titulo.texto: Bedrooms of Porfirio Díaz and Carmen Romero Rubio

frase_gancho.texto: Porfirio Díaz did not live in the Castle all year round: he used it in the summer, for balls and receptions.

puente_narrativo.texto: Move on to the presidential office, the study where Díaz kept his library.

guion_corto.texto: Before dawn, the president was already on his feet. According to the museum, Porfirio Díaz rose in the early hours, did gymnastics and swam. But he spent mostly the summer here: his family lived most of the year at number eight, La Cadena Street, today Venustiano Carranza. The Castle was adapted for balls and receptions. The couple’s bedrooms, Díaz’s and Carmen Romero Rubio’s, were imported from France. She was seventeen when she married him, and he was fifty-one, in November of eighteen eighty-one. The museum describes Carmen’s bedroom as a blend of austerity and elegance.

guion_largo.texto:
If you picture President Díaz settled in the Castle all year round, the scene needs correcting. His everyday home was on La Cadena Street, in the city center. His family lived there most of the year. He received his ministers in the National Palace. The Castle was the summer place: it was adapted for balls and receptions. His routine, according to the museum, began in the early hours, with gymnastics and swimming, and in other seasons it included hunting in Querétaro, Michoacán and Jalisco.

The woman who gave a different tone to that life was Carmen Romero Rubio. She was born in eighteen sixty-four, in the midst of the war against the French Intervention, and her godfather at baptism was Sebastián Lerdo de Tejada. Her family belonged to a political current opposed to Díaz’s. Even so, in November of eighteen eighty-one they married. Díaz was a widower, he was fifty-one years old and he was the minister of Development. She was seventeen. The civil wedding took place on November 5 and the religious one two days later, in the oratory of Archbishop Pelagio Antonio de Labastida. A UNAM thesis notes that the ceremony was presented as a gesture of goodwill toward the Church.

The museum describes Carmen as educated, elegant, discreet and devout. It says she won the acceptance of sectors that did not sympathize with the government and that she improved Díaz’s public image, without getting involved in politics. Sometimes it is said that she taught him English. The same thesis found something more modest. Some English lessons, organized by Dr. Eduardo Liceaga before the wedding, are described as fruitless. They took place in the spring of eighteen eighty-one.

The couple’s bedrooms were imported from France, according to the museum. Carmen’s combines austerity and elegance, a reflection of the European taste adopted by the upper classes of the era. The couple’s rooms were on the upper floor. An interior staircase, opened during the government of Manuel González, connected them with the reception rooms and the dining room. There was also an electric elevator, for the exclusive use of the president and his family, which linked the two floors and the basement. The [Staircase of the Lions](chap_13_escalera_leones), by contrast, was for guests.

The house was full of people. Carmen and Díaz had no children, but they lived with Luz, Porfirio and Amada, his children, and with some of his sixteen grandchildren. Of Díaz’s taste for showing off the country’s progress, there also remain the stained-glass windows of the [Leaded Glass Gallery](chap_14_vitrales_emplomados), commissioned from Paris around nineteen hundred.

That world soon came to an end. Díaz resigned on May twenty-fifth, nineteen eleven. On the thirty-first he left Veracruz aboard the steamship Ypiranga with his family, and the ship reached France on June twentieth. He died in Paris on July second, nineteen fifteen, and the couple remained together until then. Carmen returned to Mexico and died in the capital in nineteen forty-four.

texto.pregunta: Myth: Porfirio Díaz lived in Chapultepec Castle throughout his entire government.
texto.respuesta: Reality: according to the National History Museum, the presidential family lived most of the year at number eight, La Cadena Street, today Venustiano Carranza, and used the Castle in the summer, adapted for balls and receptions.
